### Problem: Number of Unequal Triplets in Array {#sec-cnt-pcomp-unequal}

::: {.p-statement}
Given an array `nums` of positive integers, count the triplets of indices $i < j < k$ whose three values are **pairwise distinct**.

For `nums = [4,4,2,4,3]` the answer is $3$: the index triplets $(0,2,4)$, $(1,2,4)$ and $(2,3,4)$, each holding the values $4, 2, 3$ in some order. For `nums = [1,1,1,1,1]` the answer is $0$.

Constraints: $3 \le n \le 100$, $1 \le nums[i] \le 1000$.

Source: [LC 2475 · Number of Unequal Triplets in Array](https://leetcode.com/problems/number-of-unequal-triplets-in-array/){.solved difficulty="Easy"}
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
"All three different" is three conditions at once; its negation, "**some two are equal**", is about one value at a time. So count the complement: there are $\binom{n}{3}$ triplets in all, and a bad one has a value $v$ that occurs at least twice in it — either exactly twice (choose $2$ of the $c_v$ copies and $1$ of the other $n - c_v$ cells) or three times ($\binom{c_v}{3}$). The bad events for different $v$ are disjoint (a triplet cannot hold two different values twice each), so
$$\text{answer} = \binom{n}{3} - \sum_v \Bigl[\binom{c_v}{2}(n - c_v) + \binom{c_v}{3}\Bigr].$$
On the sample: $\binom{5}{3} = 10$, and the value $4$ ($c = 3$) spoils $3 \cdot 2 + 1 = 7$, leaving $3$. A direct count works too — walk the value groups in any order and charge each group as the **middle** of a triple, $\text{left} \cdot c \cdot \text{right}$ — and the two forms checking each other is the point of the exercise.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Test every triplet.** Three loops, three inequalities. $O(n^3)$, $161{,}700$ triplets at $n = 100$ — the intended Easy solution and our oracle.
2. **Complement by value.** Histogram the values; subtract the bad triplets of each value from $\binom{n}{3}$. $O(n + V)$.
3. **Count the good ones by groups.** Process the distinct values in any fixed order with a running count `left` of cells in earlier groups; a group of size $c$ is the middle of `left * c * (n - left - c)` good triplets. $O(n + V)$, and the same "fix the middle" product as @sec-cnt-p4, applied to groups of values instead of indices.
:::

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Test every triplet

::: {.form-next}
The definition, $O(n^3)$. At $n \le 100$ this is what you submit; the other two forms exist for the counting ideas.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

##### Python

```{python}
def uneq_brute(nums):
    n, ans = len(nums), 0
    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(i + 1, n):
            for k in range(j + 1, n):
                if nums[i] != nums[j] and nums[j] != nums[k] and nums[i] != nums[k]:
                    ans += 1
    return ans


assert uneq_brute([4, 4, 2, 4, 3]) == 3
assert uneq_brute([1, 1, 1, 1, 1]) == 0
assert uneq_brute([1, 2, 3]) == 1
```

##### C++

```cpp
int uneqBrute(vector<int>& nums) {
    int n = nums.size(), ans = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i)
        for (int j = i + 1; j < n; ++j)
            for (int k = j + 1; k < n; ++k)
                if (nums[i] != nums[j] && nums[j] != nums[k] && nums[i] != nums[k]) ++ans;
    return ans;
}
```
:::

#### Complement by value

::: {.form-next}
Count everything, subtract what is bad. A bad triplet repeats exactly one value, so the bad counts of different values never overlap and can simply be added.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

##### Python

```{python}
def uneq_complement(nums):
    n = len(nums)
    bad = 0
    for c in Counter(nums).values():
        bad += math.comb(c, 2) * (n - c) + math.comb(c, 3)   # exactly two, or all three
    return math.comb(n, 3) - bad


assert uneq_complement([4, 4, 2, 4, 3]) == 3
assert uneq_complement([1, 1, 1, 1, 1]) == 0
assert math.comb(5, 3) == 10 and math.comb(3, 2) * 2 + math.comb(3, 3) == 7
```

##### C++

```cpp
long long uneqComplement(vector<int>& nums) {
    long long n = nums.size();
    map<int, long long> cnt;
    for (int v : nums) ++cnt[v];
    long long bad = 0;
    for (auto& kv : cnt) {
        long long c = kv.second;
        bad += c * (c - 1) / 2 * (n - c) + c * (c - 1) * (c - 2) / 6;
    }
    return n * (n - 1) * (n - 2) / 6 - bad;
}
```
:::

#### Count the good ones by groups

::: {.form-next}
A good triplet takes one cell from each of three different groups. Order the groups; each good triplet has exactly one *middle* group, and that group meets `left` choices before it and `n - left - c` after it. One pass over the histogram.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

##### Python

```{python}
def uneq_groups(nums):
    n, left, ans = len(nums), 0, 0
    for c in Counter(nums).values():           # any fixed order of the groups
        ans += left * c * (n - left - c)       # this group is the middle one
        left += c
    return ans


assert uneq_groups([4, 4, 2, 4, 3]) == 3
assert uneq_groups([1, 1, 1, 1, 1]) == 0
for _ in range(300):
    arr = [random.randint(1, 5) for _ in range(random.randint(3, 12))]
    assert uneq_groups(arr) == uneq_complement(arr) == uneq_brute(arr)
```

##### C++

```cpp
long long uneqGroups(vector<int>& nums) {
    long long n = nums.size(), left = 0, ans = 0;
    map<int, long long> cnt;
    for (int v : nums) ++cnt[v];
    for (auto& kv : cnt) {
        long long c = kv.second;
        ans += left * c * (n - left - c);      // groups before x this x groups after
        left += c;
    }
    return ans;
}
```
:::

:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Test every triplet**: $O(n^3)$ time, $O(1)$ space. **Complement by value**: $O(n)$ time to build the histogram plus one pass over at most $n$ distinct values, $O(n)$ space. **Count the good ones by groups**: the same $O(n)$ time and space. The answer is at most $\binom{100}{3} = 161{,}700$; for larger $n$ the products $\binom{c}{2}(n-c)$ need 64 bits.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- All values equal: the complement removes everything, $\binom{n}{3} - \binom{n}{3} = 0$.
- All values distinct: nothing is bad, answer $\binom{n}{3}$.
- Fewer than three distinct values: the group form never has a non-empty left and right at once, so it returns $0$ with no special case.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistakes"}
- **Forgetting the all-three case.** Subtracting only $\binom{c}{2}(n - c)$ leaves the triplets made of three equal values; on `[1,1,1,1,1]` that answers $10$ instead of $0$.
- **Subtracting $\binom{c}{2}(n-2)$.** The third cell must hold a *different* value, otherwise triplets with three equal values are subtracted three times.
- **Requiring sorted groups.** The group form does not need the values sorted; any fixed order gives each good triplet exactly one middle group.
:::

**Variants.** @sec-cnt-pcomp-ball needs the complement of two overlapping bad events and so needs inclusion–exclusion; @sec-cnt-p4 fixes the middle *index* where this problem fixed the middle *group*.
